verses.text: Ahab told Jezebel all that Elijah had done, and how he had killed all the prophets with the sword.
Then Jezebel sent a messenger to Elijah, saying, “So let the gods do to me, and more also, if I don’t make your life as the life of one of them by tomorrow about this time!”
When he saw that, he arose, and ran for his life, and came to Beersheba, which belongs to Judah, and left his servant there.

But he himself went a day’s journey into the wilderness, and came and sat down under a juniper tree. Then he requested for himself that he might die, and said, “It is enough. Now, O Yahweh, take away my life; for I am not better than my fathers.”
He lay down and slept under a juniper tree; and behold, an angel touched him, and said to him, “Arise and eat!”
He looked, and behold, there was at his head a cake baked on the coals, and a jar of water. He ate and drank, and lay down again.
Yahweh’s angel came again the second time, and touched him, and said, “Arise and eat, because the journey is too great for you.”
He arose, and ate and drank, and went in the strength of that food forty days and forty nights to Horeb, God’s Mountain.
He came to a cave there, and camped there; and behold, Yahweh’s word came to him, and he said to him, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”

He said, “Go out, and stand on the mountain before Yahweh.” Behold, Yahweh passed by, and a great and strong wind tore the mountains, and broke in pieces the rocks before Yahweh; but Yahweh was not in the wind. After the wind there was an earthquake; but Yahweh was not in the earthquake.
After the earthquake a fire passed; but Yahweh was not in the fire. After the fire, there was a still small voice.
When Elijah heard it, he wrapped his face in his mantle, went out, and stood in the entrance of the cave. Behold, a voice came to him, and said, “What are you doing here, Elijah?”

He said, “I have been very jealous for Yahweh, the God of Armies; for the children of Israel have forsaken your covenant, thrown down your altars, and killed your prophets with the sword. I, even I only, am left; and they seek my life, to take it away.”
Yahweh said to him, “Go, return on your way to the wilderness of Damascus. When you arrive, anoint Hazael to be king over Syria.
Anoint Jehu the son of Nimshi to be king over Israel; and anoint Elisha the son of Shaphat of Abel Meholah to be prophet in your place.
He who escapes from the sword of Hazael, Jehu will kill; and he who escapes from the sword of Jehu, Elisha will kill.
Yet I reserved seven thousand in Israel, all the knees of which have not bowed to Baal, and every mouth which has not kissed him.”
So he departed from there, and found Elisha the son of Shaphat, who was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen before him, and he with the twelfth. Elijah went over to him, and put his mantle on him.
Elisha left the oxen, and ran after Elijah, and said, “Let me please kiss my father and my mother, and then I will follow you.” He said to him, “Go back again; for what have I done to you?”

He returned from following him, and took the yoke of oxen, and killed them, and boiled their meat with the instruments of the oxen, and gave to the people, and they ate. Then he arose, and went after Elijah, and served him.

footnotes.content: Fear came even to Elijah—the prophet who'd just called down fire from heaven. But notice: Ahab *told* Jezebel. He didn't hide what happened. The Lord lets our enemies speak truth they don't understand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A death threat in the form of an oath. Jezebel swore by her gods—and lost her wager with the real one. When threats come with certainty, remember: she was speaking into a future only the Lord held.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He ran south to Beersheba—the borderland of Judah, as far as a man could go from Jezebel's throne. Beersheba means 'well of the oath,' a place of covenant memory. Even fleeing, the Lord planted him near a reminder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Under a juniper tree, Elijah asked to die. His faith felt exhausted—'I am not better than my fathers.' How gently the Lord meets us there, in the honest darkness, without scolding.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: An angel's touch while he slept. The Lord didn't debate his despair; He fed him. The very first word was 'Arise'—not condemnation, but invitation back to the journey.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Bread baked on coals, water in a jar—provision so plain, so tender, so near. The Lord feeds the prophet as a mother feeds her child. Twice Elijah ate and was strengthened.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The angel came a second time, naming what Elijah needed to hear: 'the journey is too great for you.' The Lord acknowledges our weakness—not to shame us, but to fuel us with His strength for what lies ahead.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Forty days and forty nights—echoing Moses on Sinai, echoing the wilderness wanderings. Elijah walked in the footsteps of prophets before, sustained by bread and water, to meet the God who had met them.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: At Horeb—the very mountain where Moses stood—Yahweh's word came to Elijah in a cave. The Lord brought His prophet home to the place where His voice had first been revealed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: 'I, even I only, am left.' But it wasn't true, and the Lord knew it. Sometimes in our darkest hour we forget that the kingdom does not depend on us. That's when He gently resets our eyes.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Wind tearing mountains, earthquake breaking rocks—the raw power of creation. Yet the Lord was not *there*. Elijah had to learn: the mightiest signs don't always carry the deepest word. Listen beyond the thunder.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: After all that shaking came 'a still small voice'—a whisper only heard in silence. The Lord speaks most tenderly to the exhausted. He did not need volume to reach Elijah's heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elijah wrapped his face in his mantle—the ancient gesture of reverence and awe. Even worn down, he knew whom he stood before. The Lord's whisper had called him back to himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: He gave the same answer as before: 'I alone am left.' The Lord didn't correct him harshly, but instead showed him the truth in the way only He could—by giving him a task, a successor, a reason to look beyond himself.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Go anoint Hazael king of Syria. Elijah's task wasn't to sit on the mountain forever; it was to go, to act, to anoint kings. The Lord met his despair with a commission.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Three anointings: Hazael, Jehu, and Elisha. The prophet who thought he stood alone was sent to ordain successors—to build a chain of witnesses that stretched beyond his own sight. He was never as alone as he believed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A hard word: escape from one sword only to meet another. Yet even here, the Lord was limiting the scope of judgment, naming exactly how it would unfold. Mercy and justice move together in His hands.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Seven thousand had not bowed to Baal—a number that recalls the faithful remnant promised through the prophets. The Lord always preserves a people who refuse to worship what is false. Elijah's solitude was an illusion.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha was plowing with twelve yoke of oxen—a working man, not a scribe or a priest. When Elijah put his mantle on him, the Lord chose a farmer to carry the prophetic word. Station doesn't limit what He can do.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha asked to kiss his mother and father goodbye. A tender request from a young man leaving home. Elijah's answer—'Go back again'—was not refusal but permission. The Lord honors the bonds that bind us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Elisha killed his oxen and burned his plow with their yoke—a final break from his old life. Readers today hear an echo in that burning: how we sometimes must lay down what we've built to follow where the Lord calls. The inheritance is worth the cost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
